title: Scene structure, transforms and the missing monitor arm

scenes.title: Trace requests into inspection, scripts and annotations

cues.text: At input ten, the user reported a missing right-side part and touchscreen. The agent instead diagnosed blank surfaces and buried encoder forms.
It ran the version four refinement and render scripts. The recorded result added five encoders and two active screen faces, while hiding duplicate clutter.
Input eleven asked for a manual-cited parts list. That source-reading step established part identities; it did not execute a Blender builder.
Input twelve turned that list into annotations. The version five script created eleven front and thirteen rear markers, then reopening checks verified all twenty-four.
Those executions explain the next inspection step. The annotations identified parts, but they neither discovered the missing arm nor established mechanical joints.

scenes.title: Follow the corrected diagnosis into the arm repair

cues.text: At input thirteen, the agent identified the keyboard drawer as the clearest omission. That conclusion missed the area the user meant.
Input fourteen corrected the diagnosis toward the right monitor assembly. Input fifteen clarified that the missing arm should mirror the left.
The version six repair copied three left-arm meshes into a new right collection. A separate render script checked side and front views.
The recorded save retained all twenty-four annotations. It restored visible support geometry, while hinge motion remained absent and placement still needed correction.

scenes.title: Objects, geometry and organization are different

cues.text: An imported Blender scene contains object instances, mesh datablocks, parents and collections. Each relationship answers a different question.
An object carries placement and other state; its mesh datablock supplies geometry, and multiple objects can refer to the same data.
The repair explicitly copies both the object and its mesh data, creating an independently editable right-side copy.
A collection organizes those copies and records metadata. That collection does not create a mechanical joint.
The exploded view now uses copied version eight console geometry. Colour separates the static console, both supports and the selected display wing.
In an isolated triangle fixture, editing the copied mesh left the original vertices unchanged. That checks data independence for the demonstrated copy operation.

scenes.title: Mirror the world transform around a datum

cues.text: The V06 builder selects three named left-arm mesh objects: the support volume, outer arm and inner inset.
It builds a reflection matrix that negates the world X coordinate and adds a translation called mirror sum.
In one dimension, the mapping is X prime equals mirror sum minus X. The mirror plane is halfway along that sum.
Applying the matrix to each source world matrix reflects both placement and orientation, so the chosen datum directly controls the result.
The matrix reference documents this coordinate operation. Placement still depends on choosing a justified datum; a reflection alone does not supply that evidence.

scenes.title: A symmetric copy can still be misplaced

cues.text: The user later reported that the new right arm was not correctly placed.
The retained V06 source combines outer X edges; the V08 correction instead uses the centres of the two monitor-side world ranges.
It subtracts the old mirror sum from the new one, then shifts the right-arm copies by that difference.
The saved V08 report records a movement of about twenty-six point seven millimetres. A plausible mirror was not enough to establish the correct placement.
The new file comparison independently finds the same approximate shift between the stored version six and version eight right-support vertices.

scenes.title: Bake the reflected copy without claiming closed geometry

cues.text: Before baking the corrected arm, the script makes another mesh copy if the data has multiple users.
It applies the captured world matrix to the mesh data and resets the object matrix to identity.
It then updates the data and flips polygon winding for the reflected copy.
Those operations address the transformed copy and its surface orientation. They do not fill the open arm surfaces or establish fabrication-ready geometry.
The isolated negative-determinant fixture preserves all three world-space vertex positions after baking, and records the reversed polygon order.
That check covers position and winding. It does not certify custom normals, closed surfaces or fabrication suitability.

scenes.title: Change a parent while preserving the current pose

cues.text: Parenting changes the transform relationship, so assigning a parent can change an object’s visible placement.
The parent-keep-world helper updates the view layer and copies the object’s current world matrix.
It assigns the new parent, restores that captured world matrix, and updates evaluation again.
The goal is to preserve the current pose while establishing the hierarchy that future parent motion will drive.
The teaching fixture uses a translated, rotated, uniformly scaled parent. Naive parenting changes the matrix; restoring the captured matrix keeps it within one millionth.
The control then moves the copied console assembly. This demonstration covers that initial pose and hierarchy, without generalizing to constrained or already animated objects.

scenes.title: Remove unrelated children from the moving group

cues.text: At input sixteen, three inline inspections audited both arms. The agent found no working hinges, inconsistent parentage and open surfaces.
That result made grouping and hinge controls the next dependency. Input eighteen explicitly requested the movable wing and two hinge stages.
The imported hierarchy included unrelated desk children. The repair captured their world matrices, cleared those parents and restored their placement.
Only selected supports and wing parts joined the new motion hierarchy. In this copied demonstration, the static console stays fixed while the wing moves.

scenes.title: State what the hinge coordinates actually mean

cues.text: The requested repair called for lower and upper hinge axes based on reference geometry.
The retained script describes its actual pivot positions as approximate centres of rounded silhouettes on the imported side arm.
It creates two empty objects with arrows, using coordinates in the source model’s inch-sized unit system.
Those controls define a visual rig. They are not surveyed bearing coordinates, and the code explicitly labels the result as not fabrication-ready.
The lower hinge is linked to the imported root when that root is present.
The upper hinge becomes a child of the lower stage, with its initial world position preserved.
Both arm assemblies follow the lower hinge; the selected display wing follows the upper hinge.
A change at the lower stage therefore carries the upper stage with it, while the upper stage adds its own relative rotation.
Red, green and blue arrows identify the local axes on the upper stage. The separate world axes stay fixed as the local axes follow their parent.
The script names four poses: open, intermediate, folded and locked, at frames one, forty, eighty and one hundred.
It sets lower and upper X rotations in radians, then inserts rotation keyframes for both controls.
Illustrative lock objects are shown at the final pose by keying their viewport and render visibility.
A pose named locked and a visible wire loop do not demonstrate a functioning latch, bearing forces or a dynamic simulation.

scenes.title: Trace the TimelineMarker failure and repair

cues.text: The first recorded rig attempt assigned a lower-angle custom property to a timeline marker. Checking for set-item support did not make that property assignment valid.
The archived error says: id properties not supported for this type. The original error, failed statement and exact patch are shown together.
The patch removed the property assignment and retained marker creation with its label and frame. The next rig call completed and saved a file.
Our isolated marker fixture reproduces the type error, then verifies the retained creation call. It is labelled as a new test, separate from the historical execution.
A completed retry resolved this API failure. It did not yet establish a correct folded pose, which the next diagnostic sequence makes clear.

scenes.title: Separate a successful call from a correct pose

cues.text: After the marker patch, the first completed retry still reported a folded height of roughly five hundred forty-six millimetres.
A subsequent correction still returned about five hundred thirty-five. Matrix and child-hierarchy inspections therefore continued; process completion was not accepted as pose correctness.
One diagnostic also returned a list where the Blender tool required a dictionary. Wrapping the result under a bounds key repaired that reporting failure.
The later rig event reported a folded height of one hundred eighty-two millimetres. That is the execution supporting the final historical height comparison.
The event identifiers and original log locations remain beside each stage, so the API repair, reporting repair and geometric correction cannot collapse into one success claim.

scenes.title: Test the measurement scope before trusting an envelope

cues.text: The source sets a frame and updates evaluation before collecting bounds. Its helper transforms the eight corners of each object bounding box.
That produces a conservative envelope. It is not generally the tight bounds of transformed mesh vertices, even though the historical comment calls the bounds exact.
A rotated tetrahedron demonstrates the difference: transformed box corners produce a larger Y extent than the actual transformed vertices.
A second fixture adds a modifier and measures evaluated vertices. Base mesh data and evaluated geometry are explicitly distinguished.
The teaching preflight rejects an incorrect unit scale, a singular transform and nonfinite values. The historical source-unit convention remains separately recorded.
The reported one-hundred-eighty-two millimetre height is historical evidence. These new fixtures explain measurement limits; they do not re-certify the hardware.

scenes.title: Keep visual comparison inside its evidence boundary

cues.text: At input seventeen, the alignment script fitted six landmarks to the official illustration and saved version seven without changing the console geometry.
The comparison found the major visible display groups, five encoders and both arms present. It also identified simplified controls and the smooth wrist-rest apron.
That viewpoint comparison supported visible-feature checks. It could not establish hidden geometry, a folding mechanism or continuous clearance.
The later rig retained width and depth discrepancies, approximate axes and open arm surfaces. Those remaining issues stay attached to the dimensional comparison.
The source register distinguishes the official reference, historical diagnostic renders and these newly generated Blender demonstrations at their points of use.

scenes.title: Keep every execution and every claim traceable

cues.text: All nine inputs and fifty-seven allocated execution events remain in the chapter evidence map. No source-reading or steering message is relabelled as a Blender execution.
Each narration cue now has a claim record linking its source lines, relevant historical events, applicable documentation and any new fixture or rendered shot.
The downloadable transcript retains full script paths. Original source, historical execution, new demonstration and proposed correction remain distinct evidence categories.

scenes.title: Carry a checked assembly explanation into measurement

cues.text: The revised chapter connects the corrected diagnosis to copied geometry, a measured datum correction, preserved placement and two-stage parent motion.
Blender demonstrations and isolated checks now make those operations visible, while the historical failure chain keeps intermediate wrong results in view.
The chapter validates its teaching examples and media. Human voice approval and physical one-to-one verification remain separate, unresolved questions.
The next chapter can build on these explicit coordinate, unit and evidence contracts when connecting photographs and drawings to model measurements.
